issues.issue: The preamble names the issuing entity "GPMF Trust 2007-HE1" while the cover page of the same instrument names "GreenPoint Mortgage Funding Trust 2007-HE1" as issuing entity. A court could be asked which designation identifies the contracting trust.

The recital purports to define "HELOCs" circularly and vaguely — "such HELOCs consist of certain home equity lines of credit" — with the term already used in the preceding recital and never delimited except by the word "certain". The scope of the defined pool is not fixed by the words themselves.

Definitions are imported wholesale from Appendix A to the Indenture "except as otherwise expressly provided herein or unless the context otherwise requires", so the operative meaning of key terms depends on an external document and on an undefined contextual override. Which text governs a given term is left open.

The enumerated conveyance items end in an open-ended catch-all — "any proceeds of the foregoing and any other property owned by the Trust and all other assets included or to be included in the Issuing Entity" — whose reach against the specific items (i)-(iv) is undefined. A court could be asked whether the catch-all sweeps in assets of a different kind from those listed.

Section 2.01(a) recites that the conveyance is "in consideration of the Issuing Entity's delivery of the proceeds from the sale of the Notes and the Certificates to the Sponsor", while the Preliminary Statement recites that the Depositor acquires the HELOCs from the Sponsor in consideration for the Depositor's transfer of the Certificates and Note proceeds and then acquires the Notes and Certificates from the Issuing Entity. The recited flow of consideration and the operative flow do not match.

The subsection imposes a funding and reimbursement obligation on "the Holder of the Class S Certificate", a person who is not a party and whose consent is deemed from mere acceptance of the certificate. Whether that obligation binds, and against whom the Servicer's advance may be enforced, turns on the words used.

Section 2.01(a) provides that none of the Securities Administrator, Master Servicer nor Indenture Trustee "shall be obligated or permitted to fund any such Draws", while Section 2.01(b) has the Securities Administrator agreeing to direct funds to reimburse Servicer Draw advances. The two subsections have to be reconciled on whether the Securities Administrator may participate in Draw funding at all.

The clause says only that "it is not intended that" any HELOC be a high-cost loan, which leaves open whether it is a representation, a covenant, or a mere statement of purpose carrying no remedy. The S&P reference compounds this by pointing simultaneously to the "then current" Glossary and to "Version 5.7 Revised".

Clause (v) requires "either a title insurance policy or guaranty title", a garbled and undefined alternative whose content cannot be identified from the text. What satisfies delivery under (v) is therefore uncertain.

The recording obligation is triggered only "[u]pon the occurrence of a Recordation Event", a term nowhere defined in this Agreement and left to Appendix A of the Indenture. When the Sponsor's recording duty arises turns on that undefined trigger.

The final sentence allows original documents not delivered to the Indenture Trustee or Custodian to be held by the Servicer in trust, which sits awkwardly against Section 2.01(d)'s unqualified requirement that the Sponsor deliver all listed documents on or before the Closing Date. Whether non-delivery is excused is left to be harmonised.

"Material Defect" is defined partly by circular reference — a document that "does not conform on its face to the review criteria specified in this Section" — and carries no materiality threshold despite its name. What counts as a Material Defect triggering repurchase is therefore contestable.

This paragraph makes any Material Defect repurchaseable without qualification, whereas the Final Certification paragraph of the same Section 2.02(a) requires that the Material Defect "materially and adversely affects the interests of the Noteholders, Certificateholders or the Note Insurer" before the same remedy is enforced. The two passages state different triggers for the same obligation.

The paragraph limits the Custodian's obligations "with respect to those documents described in subsections (b)(iv), (v) and (vii) of Section 2.01", but Section 2.01(b) concerns funding of Draws by the Class S Certificateholder; the document list is in Section 2.01(d). The cross-reference identifies no existing subsections.

The Repurchase Price is to be remitted "for deposit in the Collection Account", a term differing from the "Master Servicer Collection Account" used for the identical payment in Sections 2.02(b), 2.03(b) and 2.04. Which account is meant is left to construction.

Subsection (b) applies where a HELOC is purchased "in accordance with Subsections 2.02(a) or (b) above", but (b) is this very subsection, so the reference is circular and the intended trigger (probably 2.02(a) or 2.03) cannot be identified. The scope of the repurchase machinery depends on fixing that reference.

The sole-remedy sentence names the Issuing Entity, Noteholders, Certificateholders, Indenture Trustee and Owner Trustee, while the parallel sole-remedy sentences in Section 2.02(a) (Indenture Trustee, Issuer, Depositor, any Noteholder) and Section 2.03(b) (Issuing Entity, Noteholders, Indenture Trustee) list different beneficiaries and omit the Note Insurer. Whether a party absent from one list is bound by the limitation is a genuine internal inconsistency.

The sentence "[t]he obligations of the Sponsor to substitute or repurchase, as applicable, a HELOC shall be the ... sole remedy for any breach thereof" leaves "thereof" without a clear antecedent — breach of the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement, of the reps and warranties, or of the Servicing Agreement. The scope of the remedy limitation turns on that word.

The sole-remedy beneficiaries here (Issuing Entity, Indenture Trustee, Noteholders, Certificateholder) differ from those in Section 2.02(b) and Section 2.03(b), and the Note Insurer is omitted although Section 2.08 makes the Sponsor's covenants run to the Note Insurer. Whether the Note Insurer is bound by the limitation cannot be settled from one provision.

The repurchase trigger depends on a "discover[y]" of a breach that "materially and adversely affects the value of the interests" of named parties, and on "prompt written notice" — none of which is defined or measured. Whether discovery includes constructive knowledge and what makes a breach material and adverse are classic points of construction.

The closing sole-remedy sentence names only the Issuing Entity, the Noteholders and the Indenture Trustee, omitting the Certificateholders and the Note Insurer who are expressly covered by the parallel sole-remedy sentence in Section 2.02(b). The instrument does not say whether the omitted parties are limited to repurchase.

Section 2.04 directs the Sponsor to deliver the Substitute HELOC documents "in accordance with the provisions of the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Subsection 2.02(b) of this Agreement", but Section 2.02(b) contains only the repurchase-remittance and release mechanics; the document delivery requirements are in Section 2.01(d). The cross-reference points to a subsection with no such provisions.

Repurchase is barred for any HELOC "that is not in default or as to which default is not reasonably foreseeable", a double-negative formulation whose vagueness ("reasonably foreseeable" default) determines when the Opinion of Counsel condition bites. The boundary of the exception cannot be applied from the words alone.

"[T]he Indenture Trustee and the Owner Trustee shall require the Sponsor, at its option, to either (i) substitute ... or (ii) repurchase" leaves it unclear whose option is meant — the Sponsor's or the Trustees'. The choice of remedy depends on that pronoun.

The Depositor is described in the preamble and in Section 2.06(i) as a Delaware limited liability company, yet this representation speaks of its "full corporate power" and Section 2.06(iii) of "necessary corporate action". The corporate vocabulary does not fit the entity as defined.

The no-litigation representation ends with a dangling "; or", so it reads as one half of a disjunction whose other half (clause (vii)) is a sentence fragment rather than a separate representation. Whether the representation is limited to proceedings concerning the contemplated transactions depends on repairing the break.

Clause (vii) begins "with respect to any other matter which in the judgment of the Depositor will be determined adversely" and has no subject or verb of its own; as written it represents nothing. What, if anything, the Depositor warrants by it cannot be determined from the text.

The Depositor warrants that immediately before transfer each Mortgage Note and Mortgage "were not subject to an assignment or pledge", yet Section 2.01(a) and the recitals describe a chain in which the Sponsor sells and assigns the same HELOCs to the Depositor immediately beforehand. Whether that intervening assignment breaches the warranty is a question for construction.
